rationale: B wins because it is less likely to put a founder on the phone with a reporter holding an indefensible claim. A's punchiest line, "But the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone," turns workload equivalence into bodies out the door; that is how you buy yourself a correction. B still slips with "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot," but it also says "do not invent a group or a quote" and repeatedly names the missing proof instead of decorating the hole.
gaps_in_A: "But the Equivalent of 700 People Are Gone" overstates the update. The facts say the assistant handled work equivalent to 700 full-time agents; they do not say 700 people are gone or that 700 jobs were eliminated.

"The Headcount It Cut Is the Margin It's Showing Investors" asserts a causal margin story the update does not prove. Profitability, headcount decline, and AI efficiency are supplied; investor-facing margin attribution is not.
"Whether an AI Should Decide Your Klarna Payment Dispute" smuggles in 'decide.' The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that the AI decides them.
"Before this, AI-in-customer-service claims were largely vendor-produced" is invented market context. It may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
gaps_in_B: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" makes the same dangerous leap B later warns against. Handling or triaging a dispute is not the same as deciding it.

"Klarna cut average chat resolution from 11 minutes to under 2 — here's how" promises mechanism without supplied mechanism. The facts give LLM deployment and outcomes, not guardrails, workflow, or implementation detail.
"Story type: customer-story" is mislabeled. There is no customer protagonist, customer quote, or outcome story here; this is an operations/data angle until sourced otherwise.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" loops backward. The better next move is sourcing the withheld proof and running journalist-fit-check on the strongest surviving angle.
